newsitem.title: UK: British mother reclaims gift baby from friend.
newsitem.headline: British mother reclaims gift baby from friend.

text.p: A British woman who gave her new-born baby to a childless friend said on Saturday she had taken him back again because the friend could not cope.

The case sparked angry protests from "pro-life" campaigners, who urged the government to ban women from acting as surrogate mothers and criticised the two for exchanging the child like a "consumer item".

Shirley Farrell, 36, who already had six children in July when baby Thomas was born, said she had made a mistake in giving him to her best friend Liz Simons, 30. Simons had been trying to have a baby of her own for 11 years.
No money changed hands in what was seen as an act of unusual generosity when it became public three months ago.
But Farrell said her friend had buckled under the strain of coping with the baby and that she had taken him back permanently.
"I will let Liz see him if she wants, but he'll never live with her again. There's no way she's having him again. He's home now and he's staying," Farrell told reporters.
The British charity Life, which campaigns primarily against abortion, called for a new law banning women from becoming surrogate mothers, whether paid or unpaid.
A Life spokesman said the case of baby Thomas was a "lamentable story" which "shows once again what a wretched business surrogate motherhood is".
"Children are not consumer items to be used a presents for other people," the spokesman said.
British newspapers reported that Simons was undergoing treatment for depression in a psychiatric hospital.
"It just isn't worth it. In hindsight I don't think it was a good idea," Farell said.

"During the last few weeks Liz had stopped eating. She seemed in a daze and was getting skinnier and skinnier. The mental pressure of looking after a baby was obviously too much for her," Farell said.

In a policy reversal, the British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said earlier this year surrogate pregnancies were acceptable as a last resort for infertile couples when other fertility treatments have failed.
But it said that surrogacy contracts could not be enforced in law, and that such arrangements were fraught with problems.
